answer.answerText:
The **best app depends on how you’re recovering** and whether your surgeon/clinic already uses one.

## Best picks by use case

### 1. **Best if your surgical team supports it: Post Op**
It’s specifically designed for post-surgery recovery, with recovery check-ins, wound photo sharing, symptom/vitals logging, and secure messaging with your care team. That clinician connection is the biggest advantage over generic trackers. ([play.google.com](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?hl=en&id=app.postop.ai&utm_source=openai))

### 2. **Best for caregivers managing a full recovery plan: Tend**
Tend focuses on turning discharge instructions into a daily recovery schedule, with medication tracking, wound-care logging, symptom tracking, and flags for concerning symptoms. It looks especially useful if a family member is helping coordinate recovery. ([apps.apple.com](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/tend-recovery-care/id6760955362?utm_source=openai))

### 3. **Best all-purpose health tracker: CareClinic**
If you want something broader rather than surgery-specific, CareClinic has strong medication reminders plus symptom, vitals, sleep, mood, activity, appointment, and document tracking. Good if your recovery is complex or overlaps with chronic conditions. ([apps.apple.com](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/tracker-reminder-careclinic/id1455648231?ct=website_branch_default&utm_source=openai))

### 4. **Best simple med-timer for the first week after surgery: Rex**
If your main problem is staying on top of alternating pain meds, Rex is built around dose timing, reminders, history, and simple logging, with privacy-friendly on-device storage. ([apps.apple.com](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/rex-post-op-medication-timer/id6811731414?utm_source=openai))

### 5. **Best for private wound-photo tracking: EnnoTrace or Wound Companion**
If you mostly need to document incision healing with photos and reminders, these are more focused tools. EnnoTrace emphasizes on-device storage and guided wound-photo capture, while Wound Companion is centered on photo-based wound documentation. ([play.google.com](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.tamnura&utm_source=openai))

## My practical recommendation
Choose in this order:

1. **Use your hospital/surgeon’s app first** if they offer one.
2. If not, pick:
   - **Post Op** for team-connected recovery
   - **Tend** for caregiver-heavy recovery
   - **CareClinic** for detailed self-tracking
   - **Rex** if meds are the main issue

## What features matter most
Look for:
- medication reminders
- pain/symptom logging
- wound photo timeline
- appointment reminders
- ability to export or share logs with your surgeon
- privacy policy / where data is stored
- alerts that distinguish “call your surgeon” vs emergency symptoms

## Important caution
No app should replace your discharge instructions. If you have red-flag symptoms—like fever, worsening redness, pus, shortness of breath, chest pain, uncontrolled bleeding, or severe pain that’s getting worse—contact your surgeon promptly or seek urgent care.

answer.answerText:
A **typical hip arthroscopy recovery** often looks like this: crutches for about **1–2 weeks**, roughly **6 weeks of physical therapy**, and **3–6 months** before pain-free activity feels close to normal again. If microfracture or cartilage work was done, weight-bearing restrictions can last **up to 6 weeks**, and return to hard exercise can take **4–6 months** or longer. ([hss.edu](https://www.hss.edu/health-library/conditions-and-treatments/list/hip-arthroscopy?utm_source=openai))

Signs your recovery is **progressing as expected** include:
- pain and swelling that are **gradually trending down** week to week,
- improving ability to **walk, sit, sleep, and do daily activities**,
- slowly increasing **range of motion and strength** in PT,
- needing **less pain medication** over time,
- no major increase in pain after routine rehab work by the next day. These expectations are consistent with standard post-op rehab guidance from orthopedic centers. ([hss.edu](https://www.hss.edu/departments/hip-preservation-service/hip-rehabilitation?utm_source=openai))

It’s also normal to have some **ups and downs**. After hip arthroscopy, some pain can improve quickly, then temporarily flare as the joint lining heals; mild tenderness, swelling for about a week, and even temporary knee soreness from traction can happen. Full comfort often lags behind functional progress. ([hss.edu](https://www.hss.edu/health-library/conditions-and-treatments/list/hip-arthroscopy?utm_source=openai))

Call your surgeon or PT sooner if you have **red flags**, especially:
- fever, chills, drainage, increasing redness, or wound opening,
- calf pain/swelling, chest pain, or shortness of breath,
- worsening pain rather than gradual improvement,
- new numbness, weakness, or inability to bear weight,
- persistent severe limp or pain that keeps worsening with rehab. Post-op rehab guidelines specifically include screening for red flags and monitoring neurologic status and wound healing. ([hss.edu](https://www.hss.edu/HSSRehabilitationClinicalGuidelines-Hip--3.pdf?utm_source=openai))

A practical way to judge progress is to track 5 things each week:
1. pain at rest and with walking,
2. swelling,
3. limp/crutch dependence,
4. hip motion,
5. ability to do PT exercises and daily tasks.  
If those are **slowly improving overall**, recovery is usually on track even if some days are worse than others. This is an inference based on standard rehab milestones and monitoring recommendations. ([hss.edu](https://www.hss.edu/departments/hip-preservation-service/hip-rehabilitation?utm_source=openai))

One important caveat: “normal” recovery depends a lot on **what was actually done** during surgery—labral repair, bone reshaping for impingement, microfracture, capsular repair, etc. Procedures involving cartilage repair often recover more slowly. ([hss.edu](https://www.hss.edu/health-library/conditions-and-treatments/fai-femoroacetabular-impingement?utm_source=openai))

If you want, I can help you figure out whether **your specific timeline** seems normal if you tell me:
- how many days/weeks out you are,
- what procedure you had,
- whether you’re still on crutches,
- your current pain level,
- and what worries you most.

A “normal” hip arthroscopy recovery is usually **gradual, uneven, and protocol-dependent**, so the best sign you’re progressing as expected is that you’re slowly meeting your surgeon/PT milestones **without increasing pain, swelling, limp, or next-day flare-ups**. Recovery can take **several months**, and rehab is often adjusted based on exactly what was done during surgery, such as labral repair, femoroplasty, or microfracture. ([orthoinfo.org](https://www.orthoinfo.org/bodypart/hip-thigh/hip-arthroscopy/?utm_source=openai))

A useful way to judge progress is to look for these general patterns:
- **Pain trend:** pain should generally decrease over time, even if there are occasional bad days.
- **Function trend:** walking, transfers, stairs, and daily activities should become a bit easier week by week.
- **Range of motion and strength:** these should improve in a controlled way through PT, not by forcing motion.
- **Tolerance to rehab:** exercises may cause mild soreness, but you should not be having major worsening that lasts into the next day or two.
- **Gait:** you should be trending toward a smoother walk as weight-bearing restrictions are lifted.  
These ideas fit with modern rehab guidance that emphasizes **goal-based progression**, not just “the calendar.” ([arthroscopyjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com](https://arthroscopyjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/arj.70175?utm_source=openai))

Very broadly, many protocols follow an arc like this:
- **First few weeks:** protect the repair, use crutches if prescribed, control pain/swelling, begin gentle motion and early PT.
- **Weeks 4–8:** gradually improve walking, mobility, and basic muscle activation.
- **Around 2–4 months:** build strength, endurance, balance, and more normal function.
- **Later months:** return to sport or higher-level activity only after meeting functional criteria.  
Exact timelines vary a lot, especially if you had **microfracture or other additional procedures**, which often slow progression. ([uhhospitals.org](https://www.uhhospitals.org/-/media/files/services/rehabilitation/hip-arthroscopy-rehabilitation-guidelines.pdf?utm_source=openai))

Signs recovery may be **on track** include:
- less pain than before surgery, or pain that is different and steadily calming down
- better tolerance for walking and sitting
- decreasing reliance on pain meds
- improving sleep
- PT exercises becoming easier or advancing appropriately
- fewer sharp groin-catching episodes
- no major increase in swelling, redness, drainage, or fever. ([orthoinfo.org](https://www.orthoinfo.org/bodypart/hip-thigh/hip-arthroscopy/?utm_source=openai))

Signs you should **contact your surgeon or PT sooner** include:
- pain that is clearly worsening instead of improving
- inability to bear weight when you previously could
- new fever, increasing incision redness, drainage, or calf swelling
- chest pain or shortness of breath
- persistent severe groin pain, locking, or repeated painful catching
- a major setback after doing PT or stopping crutches too early. ([healthy.kaiserpermanente.org](https://healthy.kaiserpermanente.org/health-wellness/health-encyclopedia/he.hip-arthroscopy-what-to-expect-at-home.abr5003?utm_source=openai))

A simple self-check is to ask:
1. **Am I a little better than 1–2 weeks ago?**
2. **Can I do a bit more with the same or less pain?**
3. **Do flare-ups settle within about 24–48 hours?**
4. **Am I following my specific restrictions?**  
If the answers are mostly yes, that usually suggests expected progress. If not, it may still be fixable with a rehab adjustment, but it’s worth reviewing with your team. This is also an inference from rehab guidance that stresses respecting healing timelines and modifying rehab when symptoms lag or flare. ([chop.edu](https://www.chop.edu/sites/default/files/hip-arthroscopy-protocol.pdf?utm_source=openai))

The most important caveat: **your own operative details matter more than generic timelines**. Someone who had a straightforward FAI/labral procedure may progress differently from someone who also had cartilage work or pre-existing hip weakness. Your surgeon’s protocol should take priority over anything general online. ([orthoinfo.org](https://www.orthoinfo.org/bodypart/hip-thigh/hip-arthroscopy/?utm_source=openai))

- a **week-by-week “what’s usually normal” timeline**, or
- help you compare **your specific symptoms and post-op week** to common expectations.

answer.answerText:
The best sign is the overall trend: pain going down, movement improving, and you hitting the milestones your surgeon and physical therapist (PT) set. Every person's timeline is different, and it depends a lot on what was done. The exact timeline depends on what the surgeon repaired and how closely you follow your physiotherapy plan. So compare yourself against your own rehab plan, not just general guides.

## Rough milestones

**Weeks 0–2**
- Pain is usually severe during the first few days and often improves within 1 to 2 weeks.
- Swelling usually peaks 3 to 5 days after surgery and then starts to go down.
- Stitches are usually removed after 7 to 10 days.

**Weeks 2–6**
- Most people use crutches for 2–4 weeks to limit weight on the hip while it heals. This can be longer if you had a repair that needs more protection.
- Driving: you should be able to walk comfortably without crutches, be off pain medication, control the car safely, and make an emergency stop without significant hip pain. One meta-analysis puts this around four weeks.
- One movement target cited from the International Society for Hip Arthroscopy (ISHA) for the end of the early phase is 90 degrees of pain-free hip flexion and 10 degrees of extension. Ask your PT what your own targets are.

**Weeks 6–12**
- Rehab usually moves on to strengthening the muscles around the hip, pelvis, and core.
- Most patients walk normally by week 12.
- If your day-to-day pain is still around 4–5 out of 10 at this point, it isn't necessarily structural — hip flexor irritation and post-operative bursitis are common — but it's worth raising with your physiotherapist or surgeon.

**3–12 months**
- Hip pain should significantly diminish or disappear in three to six months.
- Going back to running or sports can take longer. It can take up to 12 months to fully return to sport. For the hip to feel truly normal, twelve months is the honest answer for most people.

## Things that are usually normal
- Some pain can come back as the irritated joint lining heals, and the hip and knee may be tender for a while from the traction used during surgery.
- You may feel like there's water in the hip or hear gurgling from the surgical fluid. Your body absorbs this quickly.
- Bruising and swelling in the buttock, hip, and groin, plus feeling very tired in the first few weeks.
- Numbness or altered feeling in the groin or genital area, caused by the traction. This is usually temporary, but mention it to your surgeon.

## Call your surgical team promptly if you have:
- More redness, warmth, or drainage around an incision, fever or chills, severe or worsening hip pain, new or worsening numbness or weakness, or swelling in the leg that won't go away or keeps growing
- Pain in your calf, thigh, groin, or the back of your knee. This can be a sign of a blood clot, so get help quickly.
- Bleeding that soaks through the bandage, red streaks running up from the incisions, or pain that doesn't get better with your pain medication
- Any shortness of breath or chest pain. Go to emergency care right away, because a clot can travel to the lungs.

## Signs to bring up at your follow-up
Groin pain that persists or gets worse, clicking, or catching can mean the surgery didn't fix the source of your symptoms. Locking, where your hip catches or locks during movement, is another one to mention. Long-lasting pain can also come from inflammation, scar tissue, or putting too much load on the joint too early.

**Tips:** Keep a simple weekly log of your pain at rest and when walking, how far you can walk, and how far you can move the hip. Your PT can measure movement at each visit. Some ups and downs are normal, especially when you start a new rehab phase. What matters is whether things are improving over several weeks, not day to day.

answer.answerText:
Yes, but **very few apps appear to do this in a rigorous, research-backed way**.

What I found:
- There are many apps for **tracking postoperative pain** and recovery, and research literature shows apps have been used to collect pain scores after surgery. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33571013/?utm_source=openai))
- A 2017 scoping review found commercially available postoperative pain apps generally had **gaps in evidence-based content** and lacked strong empirical evaluation. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5673880/?utm_source=openai))
- One current commercial example is **Steady: Post Surgery Tracker**, whose App Store listing says users can enter their procedure, surgery date, and pain level to see where they stand against a “typical recovery curve.” ([apps.apple.com](https://apps.apple.com/ca/app/steady-post-surgery-tracker/id6773054410?utm_source=openai))
- However, from the sources I found, I **could not confirm** that any consumer app is comprehensively comparing your pain against **published research norms** for each operation in a clinically validated way. Most evidence is about **monitoring**, **education**, or **communication**, not robust individualized benchmarking to the literature. ([jmir.org](https://www.jmir.org/2021/9/e25115?utm_source=openai))

So the short answer is:
- **Yes, something like this exists in limited form**.
- **No, I wouldn’t assume it is medically authoritative unless your surgeon or hospital endorses it**.

Important caution:
- Published average pain trajectories are often hard to apply to one person because pain depends on the **exact procedure, complications, anesthesia type, medications, age, prior pain conditions, and day after surgery**. Clinical guidelines emphasize structured pain assessment, but not simple consumer-app “normal pain” comparisons as a standard of care. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13001796/?utm_source=openai))

rung.query: How can I compare my surgery recovery with published patient outcomes?

answer.answerText:
A practical way is to compare **your recovery trajectory** to **published outcomes measured with the same outcome tool, at the same timepoint, in patients like you**. The key is not “How do I feel compared with anyone?” but “How do I compare with similar patients on the same scale?” ([doi.org](https://doi.org/10.1213/ANE.0000000000002758?utm_source=openai))

Here’s a step-by-step approach:

1. **Define the exact comparison group.** Match the procedure, reason for surgery, age range, baseline function, and any major risk factors or comorbidities as closely as possible. Published outcomes are only meaningful if the study population is similar to you. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10202543/?utm_source=openai))

2. **Use patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs).** Common examples are:
   - **QoR-15** for immediate postoperative recovery in the first days after surgery.
   - **PROMIS** or **WHODAS 2.0** for function, pain, and disability over weeks to months.  
   A perioperative consensus statement recommends QoR-15 early after surgery and PROMIS or WHODAS at about **30 and 90 days** if feasible. ([doi.org](https://doi.org/10.1213/ANE.0000000000002758?utm_source=openai))

3. **Compare at the same timepoint.** Day 3 pain should be compared with day 3 outcomes, not 6-week results. Published surgical recovery can vary a lot depending on whether the follow-up was postoperative day 1, discharge, 6 weeks, or 3 months. ([doi.org](https://doi.org/10.1213/ANE.0000000000002758?utm_source=openai))

4. **Look at change from your baseline, not just your current score.** If you have a pre-op score and a post-op score on the same instrument, your improvement or decline is often more informative than the raw number alone. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10202543/?utm_source=openai))

5. **Use MCID or MDC when available.**
   - **MCID** = the smallest change patients generally perceive as important.
   - **MDC** = the smallest change unlikely to be just measurement noise.  
   These concepts help decide whether your recovery is meaningfully better, worse, or essentially similar to published outcomes. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10202543/?utm_source=openai))

6. **Interpret scores correctly.** For example, **PROMIS T-scores** are standardized, and studies often report expected recovery curves or thresholds associated with likely improvement. Interpretation depends on the domain: higher scores can mean better function or worse symptoms depending on the specific PROMIS measure. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8678149/?utm_source=openai))

A simple framework you can use:

- **Baseline:** What was my function/pain before surgery?
- **Now:** What is my score today or this week?
- **Published benchmark:** What was the average or median score for similar patients at the same time?
- **Meaningful difference:** Is the gap bigger than the MCID/MDC?
- **Clinical context:** Am I also matching expected milestones like walking, self-care, sleep, or return to work? ([doi.org](https://doi.org/10.1213/ANE.0000000000002758?utm_source=openai))

Important cautions:
- Published studies often report **group averages**, which may not describe any one individual well. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-023-02237-3?utm_source=openai))
- Recovery benchmarks are **not standardized for every surgery**, so some procedures have much better comparison data than others. ([doi.org](https://doi.org/10.1213/ane.0000000000002758?utm_source=openai))
- If your recovery seems off-track, that does **not** necessarily mean a bad outcome; it may reflect different starting health, complications, rehab intensity, or study selection criteria. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10202543/?utm_source=openai))

- the **type of surgery**
